lesson.title: SCH Spelling Gym
lesson.subtitle: shoe, sheep, shoulder, shadow — the sch block in the wild

hook.title: The Block That Keeps Appearing
hook.content: The more sch words you meet, the less the three letters look strange. Schoen, schaap, schouder, schaduw: English shoe, sheep, shoulder, shadow are waiting underneath.

pattern.title: Same block, different vowel
pattern.content: The sch block stays constant; the vowel after it decides the word. Sch-oen, sch-aap, sch-ouder, sch-aduw. Read the block first, then the vowel, and the English twin usually surfaces.
pattern.trap_note: English 'sharp' has no sch, but Dutch scherp does. Not every member of the family keeps the same spelling on both sides.

exercises.prompt: Match each English meaning with its Dutch twin (SCH Spelling Gym):
exercises.target_answer: de schoen, het schaap, de schouder, scherp, de schaduw, de school
exercises.meaning: shoe, sheep, shoulder, sharp, shadow, school
exercises.explanation: These are the anchors of "SCH Spelling Gym": read each Dutch form through the pattern, not as a new word.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence says: “The shoe is black.”?
exercises.explanation: “De schoen is zwart.” is the Dutch form; the other readings bend the pattern of “SCH Spelling Gym”.

cues: The pattern: Same block, different vowel
It means: The sheep is white.
exercises.explanation: “Het schaap is wit.” puts the thought together the Dutch way — Same block, different vowel.

diagnosis.slip: an English-shaped word order slipped in
diagnosis.cue: English 'sharp' has no sch, but Dutch scherp does. Not every member of the family keeps the same spelling on both sides.

exercises.prompt: Which English sentence is built the Dutch way?
exercises.explanation: “De school is groot.” is word-for-word “The school is big.”. The odd English is the lesson — never a model to produce. Pattern: Same block, different vowel.

exercises.prompt: Listen and write the whole sentence.
cues: It means: The shadow is long.
exercises.explanation: “De schaduw is lang.” reuses only material taught in “SCH Spelling Gym” — Same block, different vowel.
exercises.affirmation: You heard “De schaduw is lang.” — a sentence built from the lesson's own Dutch, practising Same block, different vowel.

twist.prompt: One more, no safety net — say: “The shoulder is warm.”
twist.explanation: The same sch block now sits in a body word; the frame is unchanged.

summary.outcome: Recognise six sch words through their English twins and use them with the right article.
summary.takeaway: Repetition is hidden by changing the word, not the pattern.

schoen.etymology_derivation: English shoe and Dutch schoen are the same word.

schaap.etymology_derivation: English sheep and Dutch schaap are the same word.

schouder.etymology_derivation: English shoulder and Dutch schouder are the same word.

scherp.etymology_derivation: English sharp and Dutch scherp are the same word.

schaduw.etymology_derivation: English shadow and Dutch schaduw are the same word.

school.etymology_derivation: A Latin loan shared by both languages; Dutch spells the sk sound sch.

sch_sh.name: The SCH Bridge
sch_sh.phonetic_rule: English /ʃ/ (sh) corresponds to Dutch /sx/ (sch): ship → schip, shoe → schoen, sheep → schaap.
sch_sh.historical_linguistics: West Germanic *sk stayed a sk-like cluster in Dutch, spelled sch, while English palatalised it to sh.
sch_sh.philological_note: Dutch sch is not English sh; the ch is a voiceless velar fricative. School is a Latin loan shared by both languages.
